claim: Exposure to diets rich in sugar and fat lowers taste sensation in humans and vinegar flies.
source: From humans to vinegar flies, exposure to diets rich in sugar and fat lowers taste sensation, changes food choices, and promotes feeding.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work in the introduction section (Bartoshuk et al., 2006; Sartor et al., 2011; Ahart et al., 2019; May et al., 2019; Weiss et al., 2019; Kaufman et al., 2018)

claim: Exposure to diets rich in sugar and fat changes food choices in humans and vinegar flies.
source: From humans to vinegar flies, exposure to diets rich in sugar and fat lowers taste sensation, changes food choices, and promotes feeding.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Exposure to diets rich in sugar and fat promotes feeding in humans and vinegar flies.
source: From humans to vinegar flies, exposure to diets rich in sugar and fat lowers taste sensation, changes food choices, and promotes feeding.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: PAM DANs that innervate the β'2 compartment of the mushroom body respond to sweet taste.
source: We characterized a population of protocerebral anterior medial dopaminergic neurons (PAM DANs) that innervates the β'2 compartment of the mushroom body and responds to sweet taste.
evidence: Demonstrated through calcium imaging experiments showing responses to sucrose stimulation (Figure 2B)

claim: In animals fed a high sugar diet, the response of PAM-β'2 to sweet stimuli was reduced.
source: In animals fed a high sugar diet, the response of PAM-β'2 to sweet stimuli was reduced and delayed, and sensitive to the strength of the signal transmission out of the sensory neurons.
evidence: Demonstrated through calcium imaging showing decreased peak responses in SD vs CD animals (Figure 2B)

claim: In animals fed a high sugar diet, the response of PAM-β'2 to sweet stimuli was delayed.
source: In animals fed a high sugar diet, the response of PAM-β'2 to sweet stimuli was reduced and delayed, and sensitive to the strength of the signal transmission out of the sensory neurons.
evidence: Demonstrated through calcium imaging showing ~600 millisecond delay in peak responses (Figure 2C)

claim: PAM-β'2 DANs activity controls feeding rate.
source: We found that PAM-β'2 DANs activity controls feeding rate and satiation: closed-loop optogenetic activation of β'2 DANs restored normal eating in animals fed high sucrose.
evidence: Demonstrated through closed-loop optogenetic experiments showing normalized feeding rate (Figure 5B)

claim: PAM-β'2 DANs activity controls satiation.
source: We found that PAM-β'2 DANs activity controls feeding rate and satiation: closed-loop optogenetic activation of β'2 DANs restored normal eating in animals fed high sucrose.
evidence: Demonstrated through closed-loop optogenetic experiments showing normalized meal duration and post-peak feeding duration (Figure 4C, 4D)

claim: Closed-loop optogenetic activation of β'2 DANs restored normal eating in animals fed high sucrose.
source: We found that PAM-β'2 DANs activity controls feeding rate and satiation: closed-loop optogenetic activation of β'2 DANs restored normal eating in animals fed high sucrose.
evidence: Demonstrated through optoFLIC experiments showing normalized feeding behavior (Figure 4A-D)

claim: Diet-dependent alterations in taste weaken satiation by impairing the central processing of sensory signals.
source: These data argue that diet-dependent alterations in taste weaken satiation by impairing the central processing of sensory signals.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of imaging data showing reduced PAM-β'2 responses and optogenetic rescue experiments

claim: Consumption of diets high in sugar and fat decreases the perception of taste stimuli in humans and rodents.
source: Consumption of diets high in sugar and fat decreases the perception of taste stimuli, influencing food preference and promoting food intake (Bartoshuk et al., 2006; Sartor et al., 2011; Ahart et al., 2019; May et al., 2019; Weiss et al., 2019; Kaufman et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Consumption of diets high in sugar and fat influences food preference.
source: Consumption of diets high in sugar and fat decreases the perception of taste stimuli, influencing food preference and promoting food intake (Bartoshuk et al., 2006; Sartor et al., 2011; Ahart et al., 2019; May et al., 2019; Weiss et al., 2019; Kaufman et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Consumption of diets high in sugar and fat promotes food intake.
source: Consumption of diets high in sugar and fat decreases the perception of taste stimuli, influencing food preference and promoting food intake (Bartoshuk et al., 2006; Sartor et al., 2011; Ahart et al., 2019; May et al., 2019; Weiss et al., 2019; Kaufman et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Orosensory signals determine the palatability or 'liking' for foods.
source: Orosensory signals determine the palatability or 'liking' for foods (Berridge and Kringelbach, 2015), but they also promote meal termination via a process called 'sensory-enhanced (or mediated) satiety' (Chambers et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Berridge and Kringelbach, 2015

claim: Orosensory signals promote meal termination via a process called 'sensory-enhanced (or mediated) satiety'.
source: Orosensory signals determine the palatability or 'liking' for foods (Berridge and Kringelbach, 2015), but they also promote meal termination via a process called 'sensory-enhanced (or mediated) satiety' (Chambers et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chambers et al., 2015

claim: Foods that provide longer and more intense sensory exposure are more satiating.
source: Indeed, foods that provide longer and more intense sensory exposure are more satiating, reducing hunger and subsequent test-meal intake in humans (Yeomans, 2017; Bolhuis et al., 2011; Ramaekers et al., 2014; Viskaal-van Dongen et al., 2011; Cecil et al., 1998; Forde et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior human studies

claim: Foods that provide longer and more intense sensory exposure reduce hunger in humans.
source: Indeed, foods that provide longer and more intense sensory exposure are more satiating, reducing hunger and subsequent test-meal intake in humans (Yeomans, 2017; Bolhuis et al., 2011; Ramaekers et al., 2014; Viskaal-van Dongen et al., 2011; Cecil et al., 1998; Forde et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior human studies

claim: Foods that provide longer and more intense sensory exposure reduce subsequent test-meal intake in humans.
source: Indeed, foods that provide longer and more intense sensory exposure are more satiating, reducing hunger and subsequent test-meal intake in humans (Yeomans, 2017; Bolhuis et al., 2011; Ramaekers et al., 2014; Viskaal-van Dongen et al., 2011; Cecil et al., 1998; Forde et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior human studies

claim: Sensory signals function early in the satiety cascade by promoting satiation and bringing the on-going eating episode to an end.
source: Specifically, sensory signals are thought to function early in the satiety cascade (Blundell et al., 1987) by promoting satiation and bringing the on-going eating episode to an end (Blundell et al., 2010; Bellisle and Blundell, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Blundell et al., 1987; Blundell et al., 2010; Bellisle and Blundell, 2013

claim: Nutrient-derived signals develop more slowly than sensory signals.
source: This is in contrast to nutrient-derived signals, which develop more slowly and consolidate satiety by inhibiting further eating after the end of a meal (Blundell et al., 2010; Bellisle and Blundell, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Blundell et al., 2010; Bellisle and Blundell, 2013

claim: Nutrient-derived signals consolidate satiety by inhibiting further eating after the end of a meal.
source: This is in contrast to nutrient-derived signals, which develop more slowly and consolidate satiety by inhibiting further eating after the end of a meal (Blundell et al., 2010; Bellisle and Blundell, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Blundell et al., 2010; Bellisle and Blundell, 2013

claim: D. melanogaster flies exposed to palatable diets rich in sugar or fat overconsume.
source: Like humans and rodents, D. melanogaster flies exposed to palatable diets rich in sugar or fat overconsume, gain weight, and become at-risk for obesity and develop phenotypes associated with metabolic syndrome (Musselman and Kühnlein, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Musselman and Kühnlein, 2018

claim: D. melanogaster flies exposed to palatable diets rich in sugar or fat gain weight.
source: Like humans and rodents, D. melanogaster flies exposed to palatable diets rich in sugar or fat overconsume, gain weight, and become at-risk for obesity and develop phenotypes associated with metabolic syndrome (Musselman and Kühnlein, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Musselman and Kühnlein, 2018

claim: D. melanogaster flies exposed to palatable diets rich in sugar or fat become at-risk for obesity.
source: Like humans and rodents, D. melanogaster flies exposed to palatable diets rich in sugar or fat overconsume, gain weight, and become at-risk for obesity and develop phenotypes associated with metabolic syndrome (Musselman and Kühnlein, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Musselman and Kühnlein, 2018

claim: D. melanogaster flies exposed to palatable diets rich in sugar or fat develop phenotypes associated with metabolic syndrome.
source: Like humans and rodents, D. melanogaster flies exposed to palatable diets rich in sugar or fat overconsume, gain weight, and become at-risk for obesity and develop phenotypes associated with metabolic syndrome (Musselman and Kühnlein, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Musselman and Kühnlein, 2018

claim: Consumption of high dietary sugar decreased the electrophysiological and calcium responses of the Gr64f+ sweet sensing neurons to sweet stimuli.
source: We recently showed that, in addition to promoting feeding by increasing meal size, consumption of high dietary sugar decreased the electrophysiological and calcium responses of the Gr64f+ sweet sensing neurons to sweet stimuli, independently of weight gain (May et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to May et al., 2019

claim: Consumption of high dietary sugar decreased the responses of Gr64f+ sweet sensing neurons to sweet stimuli independently of weight gain.
source: We recently showed that, in addition to promoting feeding by increasing meal size, consumption of high dietary sugar decreased the electrophysiological and calcium responses of the Gr64f+ sweet sensing neurons to sweet stimuli, independently of weight gain (May et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to May et al., 2019

claim: Physiological changes in the Gr64f+ cells reduced the fruit flies' taste sensitivity and response intensity.
source: These physiological changes in the Gr64f+ cells reduced the fruit flies' taste sensitivity and response intensity.
evidence: Inferred from prior work cited (May et al., 2019)

claim: Opto- and neurogenetics manipulations to correct the responses of the Gr64f+ neurons to sugar prevented animals exposed to high dietary sugar from overfeeding.
source: Opto- and neurogenetics manipulations to correct the responses of the Gr64f+ neurons to sugar prevented animals exposed to high dietary sugar from overfeeding and restored normal meal size (May et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to May et al., 2019

claim: Opto- and neurogenetics manipulations to correct the responses of the Gr64f+ neurons to sugar restored normal meal size in animals exposed to high dietary sugar.
source: Opto- and neurogenetics manipulations to correct the responses of the Gr64f+ neurons to sugar prevented animals exposed to high dietary sugar from overfeeding and restored normal meal size (May et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to May et al., 2019

claim: The diet-dependent dulling in sweet taste causes higher feeding in flies.
source: Thus, the diet-dependent dulling in sweet taste causes higher feeding in flies, but how does this happen?
evidence: Inferred from prior work and experiments in this study

claim: Dopaminergic circuits process sweet taste information in humans, rodents, and fruit flies.
source: Indeed, while the neural pathways that bring sensory information from the periphery to higher order brain regions are unique across organisms, dopaminergic circuits process sweet taste information in humans, rodents, and fruit flies.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about dopaminergic processing across species

claim: The reinforcing effects of sugar taste and nutrient properties are relayed via distinct dopaminergic pathways in humans, rodents, and fruit flies.
source: Interestingly, the reinforcing effects of sugar taste and nutrient properties are relayed via distinct dopaminergic pathways in these organisms (Yamagata et al., 2015; Huetteroth et al., 2015; Tellez et al., 2016; Thanarajah et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yamagata et al., 2015; Huetteroth et al., 2015; Tellez et al., 2016; Thanarajah et al., 2019

claim: DANs in the Protocerebral Anterior Medial (PAM) cluster respond to the sweet sensory properties to signal sugar reward in flies.
source: In flies, DANs in the Protocerebral Anterior Medial (PAM) cluster respond to the sweet sensory properties to signal sugar reward (Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012), reinforce short term appetitive memories (Yamagata et al., 2015; Huetteroth et al., 2015), and promote foraging and intake (Tsao et al., 2018; Musso et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012

claim: PAM DANs reinforce short term appetitive memories in flies.
source: In flies, DANs in the Protocerebral Anterior Medial (PAM) cluster respond to the sweet sensory properties to signal sugar reward (Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012), reinforce short term appetitive memories (Yamagata et al., 2015; Huetteroth et al., 2015), and promote foraging and intake (Tsao et al., 2018; Musso et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yamagata et al., 2015; Huetteroth et al., 2015

claim: PAM DANs promote foraging and intake in flies.
source: In flies, DANs in the Protocerebral Anterior Medial (PAM) cluster respond to the sweet sensory properties to signal sugar reward (Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012), reinforce short term appetitive memories (Yamagata et al., 2015; Huetteroth et al., 2015), and promote foraging and intake (Tsao et al., 2018; Musso et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tsao et al., 2018; Musso et al., 2019

claim: The synaptobrevin-pHluorin fluorescent changes upon sugar presentation were markedly decreased when flies were fed a high sugar diet for 7 days.
source: We found that the syb-pHluorin fluorescent changes upon sugar presentation were markedly decreased when flies were fed a high sugar diet (SD, 30% sucrose) for 7 days, compared to age-matched flies fed a control diet (CD,~8% sucrose) (Figure 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through in vivo imaging of syb-pHluorin in Gr64f+ neurons (Figure 1B)

claim: Both the responses of the sweet sensing Gr64f+ neurons to sugar and the transmission of the sweet taste signal are decreased by exposure to the SD.
source: These data suggest that both the responses of the sweet sensing Gr64f+ neurons to sugar and the transmission of the sweet taste signal are decreased by exposure to the SD.
evidence: Inferred from syb-pHluorin imaging data showing decreased vesicular release (Figure 1)

claim: DANs in the Protocerebral Anterior Medial (PAM) cluster that are labeled by the R48B04-GAL4 transgene and innervate the β'2 and γ4 compartments of the Mushroom Body respond to sweet sensory properties.
source: In flies, DANs in the Protocerebral Anterior Medial (PAM) cluster that are labeled by the R48B04-GAL4 transgene and innervate the β'2 and γ4 compartments of the Mushroom Body (MB), respond to sweet sensory properties (Huetteroth et al., 2015; Yamagata et al., 2015); neurons of this population also centrally reinforce water taste (Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huetteroth et al., 2015; Yamagata et al., 2015

claim: Neurons in the PAM cluster labeled by R48B04-GAL4 centrally reinforce water taste.
source: In flies, DANs in the Protocerebral Anterior Medial (PAM) cluster that are labeled by the R48B04-GAL4 transgene and innervate the β'2 and γ4 compartments of the Mushroom Body (MB), respond to sweet sensory properties (Huetteroth et al., 2015; Yamagata et al., 2015); neurons of this population also centrally reinforce water taste (Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lin et al., 2014

claim: The β'2 compartment is involved in processing of the taste properties alone.
source: Here we focused on the β'2 compartment because of its role in processing of the taste properties alone, compared to γ4 which is modulated by both taste and additional factors, such as internal state (Lin et al., 2014; Yamagata et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lin et al., 2014; Yamagata et al., 2015

claim: The γ4 compartment is modulated by both taste and additional factors, such as internal state.
source: Here we focused on the β'2 compartment because of its role in processing of the taste properties alone, compared to γ4 which is modulated by both taste and additional factors, such as internal state (Lin et al., 2014; Yamagata et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lin et al., 2014; Yamagata et al., 2015

claim: R48B04 is expressed in other neurons, including the Pars Intercelebralis.
source: In addition to labeling ~60 DANs in each PAM cluster, R48B04 is expressed in other neurons, including the Pars Intercelebralis.
evidence: Based on anatomical characterization of the GAL4 line

claim: The split-GAL4 line MB301B labels ~12 TH+ PAM-β2β'2a neurons.
source: We selected the split-GAL4 line MB301B which had been implicated in foraging and feeding (Tsao et al., 2018; Musso et al., 2019) and which labels ~12 TH+ PAM-β2β'2a and only shows a few, sparse projections in the ventral nerve cord and SEZ (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated through immunofluorescence staining with anti-TH antibody (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)

claim: MB301B has been implicated in foraging and feeding.
source: We selected the split-GAL4 line MB301B which had been implicated in foraging and feeding (Tsao et al., 2018; Musso et al., 2019) and which labels ~12 TH+ PAM-β2β'2a and only shows a few, sparse projections in the ventral nerve cord and SEZ (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tsao et al., 2018; Musso et al., 2019

claim: MB301B neurons respond to stimulation of the labellum with 30% sucrose.
source: We used the presynaptically targeted GCaMP6s::Bruchpilot::mCherry (Kiragasi et al., 2017) to record the response of MB301B neurons to stimulation of the labellum with 30% sucrose. We observed an increase in signal in the β'2compartment (rose), showing that these PAM-β'2 neurons process sweet sensory information (Figure 2B, grey lines; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated through calcium imaging (Figure 2B)

claim: The responses of MB301B neurons to sucrose taste in flies fed a SD for 7 days showed a nearly 50% decrease.
source: Next we measured the responses of MB301B neurons to sucrose taste in flies fed a SD for 7 days and we found a nearly 50% decrease (Figure 2B, rose lines; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated through calcium imaging comparing CD and SD animals (Figure 2B)

claim: There is a ~ 600 millisecond delay in the peak responses to the sucrose stimulus delivery to the labellum in flies fed a SD.
source: Furthermore, when we looked at both the average and individual traces, we saw a ~ 600 millisecond delay in the peak responses to the sucrose stimulus delivery to the labellum (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated through calcium imaging latency analysis (Figure 2C)

claim: A decrease in calcium responses occurred when the proboscis was stimulated with 5% sucrose in flies fed a SD.
source: A decrease in calcium responses also occurred when the proboscis was stimulated with a lower concentration of sucrose (5%), but we did not find a delayed response, suggesting that the changes in the timing of the processing may be unique to higher sugar concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated through calcium imaging with 5% sucrose (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)

claim: No delayed response was found when the proboscis was stimulated with 5% sucrose in flies fed a SD.
source: A decrease in calcium responses also occurred when the proboscis was stimulated with a lower concentration of sucrose (5%), but we did not find a delayed response, suggesting that the changes in the timing of the processing may be unique to higher sugar concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated through calcium imaging latency analysis with 5% sucrose (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D)

claim: No sugar taste responses were recorded in β2.
source: No sugar taste responses were recorded in β2 (green), consistent with the idea that it is not involved in taste processing (Figure 2D; Yamagata et al., 2015).
evidence: Demonstrated through calcium imaging of β2 compartment (Figure 2D) and supported by citation to Yamagata et al., 2015

claim: The central processing of sweet stimuli in PAM-β'2 MB301B neurons is both decreased and delayed by exposure to a high sugar diet.
source: Thus, the central processing of sweet stimuli in PAM-β'2 MB301B neurons is both decreased and delayed by exposure to a high sugar diet.
evidence: Inferred from calcium imaging data showing decreased and delayed responses (Figure 2B, 2C)

claim: PAM-β'2 neurons respond to water.
source: In addition to sweet stimuli, PAM-β'2 neurons also respond to water (Lin et al., 2014); we reasoned that if high dietary sugar unspecifically changed the activity of the PAM-β'2, we would expect flies on the SD to also exhibit impaired central responses to water.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lin et al., 2014

claim: The magnitude and timing of the β'2 response to water stimulation of the labellum were unchanged between flies on a CD or SD.
source: However, the magnitude and timing of the β'2 response to water stimulation of the labellum were unchanged between flies on a CD or SD (Figure 3A,B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; water stimulation was delivered in the same flies as in Figure 2).
evidence: Demonstrated through calcium imaging with water stimulation (Figure 3A, 3B)

claim: The decrease in PAM-β'2 responses in flies fed a SD is specific to the sweet sensory stimulus.
source: Thus, the decrease in PAM-β'2 responses in flies fed a SD is specific to the sweet sensory stimulus.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that water responses are unchanged while sucrose responses are decreased (Figure 3A, 3B)

claim: The overall ability of PAM-β'2 DANs to respond to stimuli is not generally affected by high dietary sugar.
source: This argues that the overall ability of these DANs to respond to stimuli is not generally affected, and the reduction observed on a SD could occur because of the diet-dependent changes in the sweet taste neurons in the periphery (May et al., 2019 and Figure 1).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that water responses are unchanged (Figure 3A, 3B) and supported by prior work (May et al., 2019)

claim: A high fat diet (FD) has the same caloric content as the high sugar diet (SD).
source: To further probe this question, we fed flies a high fat diet (FD), which has the same caloric content of the high sugar diet (SD) and promotes fat accumulation, but does not decrease the responses of the Gr64f+ sensory neurons to sugar stimuli (May et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on experimental diet composition described in Materials and methods

claim: A high fat diet promotes fat accumulation.
source: To further probe this question, we fed flies a high fat diet (FD), which has the same caloric content of the high sugar diet (SD) and promotes fat accumulation, but does not decrease the responses of the Gr64f+ sensory neurons to sugar stimuli (May et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to May et al., 2019

claim: A high fat diet does not decrease the responses of the Gr64f+ sensory neurons to sugar stimuli.
source: To further probe this question, we fed flies a high fat diet (FD), which has the same caloric content of the high sugar diet (SD) and promotes fat accumulation, but does not decrease the responses of the Gr64f+ sensory neurons to sugar stimuli (May et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to May et al., 2019

claim: A FD diet had no effect on the PAM-β'2 responses to sucrose stimulation of the labellum in MB301B > GCaMP6s::Bruchpilot::mCherry flies.
source: However, a FD diet had no effect on the PAM-β'2 responses to sucrose or water stimulation of the labellum in MB301B > GCaMP6s::Bruchpilot::mCherry flies (Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Demonstrated through calcium imaging comparing CD and FD animals (Figure 3C, 3D)

claim: A FD diet had no effect on the PAM-β'2 responses to water stimulation of the labellum in MB301B > GCaMP6s::Bruchpilot::mCherry flies.
source: However, a FD diet had no effect on the PAM-β'2 responses to sucrose or water stimulation of the labellum in MB301B > GCaMP6s::Bruchpilot::mCherry flies (Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Demonstrated through calcium imaging comparing CD and FD animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, 1C)

claim: The dysfunction in the processing of sweet taste stimuli in the PAM-β'2 neurons of flies on a SD is linked to alterations in the peripheral sensory processing of sugar taste caused by high dietary sugar.
source: Together, these two lines of evidence argue that the dysfunction in the processing of sweet taste stimuli in the PAM-β'2 neurons of flies on a SD is linked to alterations in the peripheral sensory processing of sugar taste caused by high dietary sugar.
evidence: Inferred from the specificity of responses to sweet vs water and SD vs FD (Figure 3A-D)

claim: OGT is responsible for decreasing sweet taste on a SD.
source: To rescue the sweet taste deficits caused by a high sugar diet we fed flies an inhibitor of the metabolic-signalling enzyme O-GlcNAc-Transferase (OGT), which we previously found to be responsible for decreasing sweet taste on a SD (May et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to May et al., 2019

claim: Supplementing the flies' diet with 75 µM of OSMI-1 resulted in no changes in PER between a CD and SD.
source: In accordance with our previous findings on OGT (May et al., 2019), supplementing the flies' diet with 75 µM of OSMI-1 (OGT-small molecule inhibitor 1) resulted in no changes in PER between a CD and SD (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated through PER assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D)

claim: The calcium responses of PAM-β'2 neurons to sucrose stimulation of the labellum were identical in SD+OSMI and CD+OSMI flies.
source: In these flies, the calcium responses of PAM-β'2 neurons to sucrose stimulation of the labellum were identical in SD+OSMI and CD+OSMI flies.
evidence: Demonstrated through calcium imaging with OSMI-1 supplementation (Figure 3E, 3F)

claim: Deficits in the peripheral responses drive impairments in the central processing of sweetness.
source: Although we cannot exclude the possibility that the OGT inhibitor also acted elsewhere outside the sensory neurons, our data support the idea that deficits in the peripheral responses drive impairments in the central processing of sweetness (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Inferred from OSMI-1 rescue experiments (Figure 3E, 3F)

claim: The impairments in the central processing of sweet sensory information by DANs are mediated by deficits in peripheral sweet taste responses.
source: Together, these orthogonal lines of evidence suggest that the impairments in the central processing of sweet sensory information by DANs are mediated by deficits in peripheral sweet taste responses.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including water vs sucrose responses, FD vs SD, and OSMI-1 rescue

claim: A diet-dependent dulling of sweet taste drives higher feeding behavior and weight gain by increasing the size and duration of meals.
source: We previously showed that a diet-dependent dulling of sweet taste drives higher feeding behavior and weight gain by increasing the size and duration of meals (May et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to May et al., 2019

claim: MB301B > ReaChR flies that did not receive retinal supplementation exhibited the characteristic increase in feeding behavior on 20% sucrose.
source: MB301B > ReaChR flies that did not receive retinal supplementation (ATR, all-trans-retinal is required to form a functional light-sensitive opsin) exhibited the characteristic increase in feeding behavior on 20% sucrose (Figure 4A, rose line); however, MB301B > ReaChR +ATR animals, which were activated by light, had stable feeding for 10 days (Figure 4A, peach line).
evidence: Demonstrated through optoFLIC experiments (Figure 4A)

claim: MB301B > ReaChR +ATR animals, which were activated by light, had stable feeding for 10 days on 20% sucrose.
source: MB301B > ReaChR flies that did not receive retinal supplementation (ATR, all-trans-retinal is required to form a functional light-sensitive opsin) exhibited the characteristic increase in feeding behavior on 20% sucrose (Figure 4A, rose line); however, MB301B > ReaChR +ATR animals, which were activated by light, had stable feeding for 10 days (Figure 4A, peach line).
evidence: Demonstrated through optoFLIC experiments (Figure 4A)

claim: Control animals on 20% sucrose had more feeding interactions per meal with more days on the SD.
source: Control animals on 20% sucrose had more feeding interactions per meal and longer meal duration with more days on the SD (Figure 4B and C, rose lines), consistent with our previous data (May et al., 2019).
evidence: Demonstrated through optoFLIC experiments (Figure 4B) and supported by citation to May et al., 2019

claim: Control animals on 20% sucrose had longer meal duration with more days on the SD.
source: Control animals on 20% sucrose had more feeding interactions per meal and longer meal duration with more days on the SD (Figure 4B and C, rose lines), consistent with our previous data (May et al., 2019).
evidence: Demonstrated through optoFLIC experiments (Figure 4C) and supported by citation to May et al., 2019

claim: A SD induced a lengthening of the peak-to-end of the meal by ~4 hr.
source: In particular, we found that a SD induced a lengthening of the peak-to-end of the meal by ~4 hr, suggesting that the satiation process is delayed in these animals (Figure 4D, rose line).
evidence: Demonstrated through optoFLIC experiments measuring post-peak feeding duration (Figure 4D)

claim: Feeding-paired stimulation of PAM-β'2 neurons stabilized the size and duration of the meal over the entire duration of the experiment.
source: However, feeding-paired stimulation of PAM-β'2 neurons stabilized the size and duration of the meal, as well as the time to satiation, over the entire duration of the experiment (Figure 4B,C and D, peach lines).
evidence: Demonstrated through optoFLIC experiments with closed-loop optogenetic stimulation (Figure 4B, 4C, 4D)

claim: Feeding-paired stimulation of PAM-β'2 neurons stabilized the time to satiation over the entire duration of the experiment.
source: However, feeding-paired stimulation of PAM-β'2 neurons stabilized the size and duration of the meal, as well as the time to satiation, over the entire duration of the experiment (Figure 4B,C and D, peach lines).
evidence: Demonstrated through optoFLIC experiments with closed-loop optogenetic stimulation (Figure 4B, 4C, 4D)

claim: Stimulation of the Gr64f+ sweet taste neurons corrected meal size and duration.
source: Interestingly, stimulation of the Gr64f+ sweet taste neurons also corrected these two aspects of meal structure (May et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to May et al., 2019

claim: Flies in which PAM-β'2 DANs were activated still developed taste deficits on a SD.
source: Importantly, flies in which these PAM-β'2 DANs were activated still developed taste deficits on a SD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), arguing against the possibility that PAM-β'2 DANs stimulation prevents increased feeding by rescuing the taste changes in the Gr64f+ neurons.
evidence: Demonstrated through PER assay in MB301B > NaChBac flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)

claim: PAM-β'2 DANs modulate meal structure and feeding behavior by integrating the sensory signal from the periphery.
source: Instead, our data suggest that PAM-β'2 DANs modulate meal structure and feeding behavior by integrating the sensory signal from the periphery.
evidence: Inferred from optogenetic rescue experiments and PER data showing taste deficits persist

claim: Identical stimulation of PAM-β'2 DANs in flies fed 5% sucrose resulted in higher feeding.
source: Interestingly, identical stimulation of PAM-β'2 DANs in flies fed 5% sucrose resulted in higher feeding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), as previously showed with both sucrose food and water (Musso et al., 2019); this indicates the the context of animal's diet and the basal activity state of PAM-β'2 DANs are important to control eating.
evidence: Demonstrated through optoFLIC experiments on 5% sucrose (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and supported by citation to Musso et al., 2019

claim: The context of animal's diet and the basal activity state of PAM-β'2 DANs are important to control eating.
source: Interestingly, identical stimulation of PAM-β'2 DANs in flies fed 5% sucrose resulted in higher feeding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), as previously showed with both sucrose food and water (Musso et al., 2019); this indicates the the context of animal's diet and the basal activity state of PAM-β'2 DANs are important to control eating.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of PAM-β'2 stimulation on CD vs SD

claim: Activation of PAM-β'2 DANs prevented diet-induced obesity in animals fed high dietary sugar.
source: In accordance with the stable feeding patterns recorded on the optoFLIC in animals fed a SD, we found that activation of PAM-β'2 DANs also prevented diet-induced obesity in animals fed high dietary sugar (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated through TAG assay in MB301B > NaChBac flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)

claim: Activation of different subpopulations of PAM-β'2 with eight distinct GAL4 transgenes failed to rescue diet-induced obesity.
source: Interestingly, PAM-β'2 DANs labeled by MB301B seem to play a unique role in this process. Activation of different subpopulations of PAM-β'2 with eight distinct GAL4 transgenes (Aso and Rubin, 2016; Aso et al., 2014b) (MB056B, MB109B, MB042B, MB032B, MB312B, MB196B, MB316B, some of these also express in γ4) failed to rescue diet-induced obesity (Figure 4—figure supplements 1D and 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated through TAG assays with multiple GAL4 lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D)

claim: Flies with activation of nutrient-responsive PAM DANs which express in β2 still accumulated fat as controls when fed high dietary sugar.
source: Further, flies with activation of nutrient-responsive PAM DANs (Yamagata et al., 2015; Huetteroth et al., 2015), which express in β2, still accumulated fat as controls when fed high dietary sugar, suggesting that effects of MB301B neuron activation come from the sweet-responsive β'2 compartment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated through TAG assay with R15A04 line (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) and supported by citations to Yamagata et al., 2015; Huetteroth et al., 2015

claim: Both the feeding events per meal and the feeding rate increased with chronic exposures to high dietary sugar.
source: We found that both the feeding events per meal and the feeding rate increased with chronic exposures to high dietary sugar (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated through optoFLIC analysis (Figure 5A, 5B)

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of PAM-β'2 prevented increases in feeding events per meal and maintained a stable number of events over the duration of the experiment.
source: However, optogenetic stimulation of PAM-β'2 prevented these increases and maintained a stable number of events and a constant feeding rate per meal over the duration of the experiment.
evidence: Demonstrated through optoFLIC analysis (Figure 5A, 5B)

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of PAM-β'2 maintained a constant feeding rate per meal over the duration of the experiment.
source: However, optogenetic stimulation of PAM-β'2 prevented these increases and maintained a stable number of events and a constant feeding rate per meal over the duration of the experiment.
evidence: Demonstrated through optoFLIC analysis (Figure 5A, 5B)

claim: The feeding rate past the peak of the meal increased with time in animals fed 20% sucrose.
source: The feeding rate past the peak of the meal increased with time in animals fed 20% sucrose, but stayed the same in flies with activation of PAM-β'2 neurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: Demonstrated through optoFLIC analysis of post-peak feeding rate (Figure 5C)

claim: The feeding rate past the peak of the meal stayed the same in flies with activation of PAM-β'2 neurons.
source: The feeding rate past the peak of the meal increased with time in animals fed 20% sucrose, but stayed the same in flies with activation of PAM-β'2 neurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: Demonstrated through optoFLIC analysis of post-peak feeding rate (Figure 5C)

claim: The pre-peak eating increased gradually with exposure to high dietary sugar.
source: Interestingly, the pre-peak eating also increased gradually with exposure to high dietary sugar (Figure 5D).
evidence: Demonstrated through optoFLIC analysis of pre-peak feeding rate (Figure 5D)

claim: Diet-dependent impairments in PAM-β'2 neurons promote overfeeding by impairing satiation.
source: Together, these data suggest that diet-dependent impairments in PAM-β'2 neurons promote overfeeding by impairing satiation, and specifically by affecting the feeding rate during a meal.
evidence: Inferred from feeding rate analysis and optogenetic rescue experiments

claim: Diet-dependent impairments in PAM-β'2 neurons promote overfeeding by affecting the feeding rate during a meal.
source: Together, these data suggest that diet-dependent impairments in PAM-β'2 neurons promote overfeeding by impairing satiation, and specifically by affecting the feeding rate during a meal.
evidence: Inferred from feeding rate analysis and optogenetic rescue experiments

claim: The central processing of sensory experiences during a meal by PAM-β'2 DANs controls feeding rate and sensory-enhanced satiation.
source: Together we propose that the central processing of sensory experiences during a meal by PAM-β'2 DANs, controls feeding rate and sensory-enhanced satiation.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of imaging and behavioral experiments

claim: The central processing of sensory experiences during a meal by PAM-β'2 DANs is altered by high dietary sugar, leading to an attenuated satiation process and higher feeding.
source: This process is altered by high dietary sugar, leading to an attenuated satiation process and higher feeding (Figure 5E).
evidence: Inferred from the combination of imaging and behavioral experiments, summarized in model (Figure 5E)

claim: Diet-dependent changes in sensory perception promote feeding and weight gain by impairing the central dopaminergic processing of sweet taste information.
source: In this study we found that diet-dependent changes in sensory perception promote feeding and weight gain by impairing the central dopaminergic processing of sweet taste information.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of all experimental results in the study

claim: When animals consume a high sugar diet, the responses to sweet taste of a distinct population of PAM DANs innervating the β'2 compartment of the MB are decreased and delayed.
source: When animals consume a high sugar diet, the responses to sweet taste of a distinct population of PAM DANs innervating the β'2 compartment of the MB are decreased and delayed.
evidence: Demonstrated through calcium imaging experiments (Figure 2B, 2C)

claim: Alterations in dopaminergic processing increase the eating rate and extend the duration of meals, leading to attenuated satiation, higher feeding, and weight gain.
source: These alterations in dopaminergic processing increase the eating rate and extend the duration of meals, leading to attenuated satiation, higher feeding, and weight gain (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated through optoFLIC experiments and TAG assays

claim: Animals fed high dietary sugar exhibited differences in PAM-β'2 responses to sweet, but not water taste stimuli.
source: Similarly, animals fed high dietary sugar exhibited differences in PAM-β'2 responses to sweet, but not water taste stimuli, reinforcing the idea that PAM DAN alterations occur because of lower signal transmission from the sensory neurons (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated through calcium imaging with sweet and water stimuli (Figure 2, Figure 3A, 3B)

claim: Correcting sweet taste deficits by feeding fruit flies an inhibitor of the enzyme O-GlcNAc Transferase prevented impairments in PAM-β'2 responses.
source: Indeed, correcting sweet taste deficits by feeding fruit flies an inhibitor of the enzyme O-GlcNAc Transferase – which we previously found to be required for taste impairments– prevented impairments in PAM-β'2 responses, although we cannot exclude that this could also be due to its effect beyond the sensory neurons (but not in the MB301B neurons, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated through calcium imaging with OSMI-1 supplementation (Figure 3E, 3F) and TAG assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A)

claim: Diet-dependent changes in taste intensity and sensitivity reduce the central processing of sensory stimuli to cause weaker and attenuated satiation.
source: Here, we propose a model where diet-dependent changes in taste intensity and sensitivity reduce the central processing of sensory stimuli to cause weaker and attenuated satiation.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of all experimental results

claim: MB301B is largely distinct from other PAM-β'2 lines both ventrally and anteriorly.
source: MB301B is largely distinct from these other lines both ventrally and anteriorly.
evidence: Based on anatomical comparison of GAL4 lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A)

claim: Ventral expression of MB301B enters the β2 compartment, which has been implicated in nutrient reward.
source: Ventral expression of MB301B enters the β2 compartment, which has been implicated in nutrient reward; however, this compartment is not responsive to sweetness and its activation still resulted in diet-induced obesity.
evidence: Based on anatomical analysis and TAG assay results (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E)

claim: The β2 compartment is not responsive to sweetness.
source: Ventral expression of MB301B enters the β2 compartment, which has been implicated in nutrient reward; however, this compartment is not responsive to sweetness and its activation still resulted in diet-induced obesity.
evidence: Demonstrated through calcium imaging (Figure 2D) and supported by prior knowledge

claim: Neurogenetic or closed-loop optogenetic activation of MB301B PAM-β2β'2 neurons resulted in an increase in foraging behavior.
source: Interestingly, two studies previously found that neurogenetic or closed-loop optogenetic activation of MB301B PAM-β2β'2 neurons resulted in an increase in foraging behavior (Tsao et al., 2018) and higher feeding to both water and sucrose substrates (Musso et al., 2019), respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsao et al., 2018

claim: Closed-loop optogenetic activation of MB301B PAM-β2β'2 neurons resulted in higher feeding to both water and sucrose substrates.
source: Interestingly, two studies previously found that neurogenetic or closed-loop optogenetic activation of MB301B PAM-β2β'2 neurons resulted in an increase in foraging behavior (Tsao et al., 2018) and higher feeding to both water and sucrose substrates (Musso et al., 2019), respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation to Musso et al., 2019

claim: Closed-loop optogenetic activation of MB301B neurons in flies fed a control diet (5% sucrose) resulted in higher feeding.
source: We also measured an increase in feeding behavior with closed-loop optogenetic activation of MB301B neurons in flies fed a control diet (5% sucrose), confirming these observations.
evidence: Demonstrated through optoFLIC experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)

claim: Applying the same optogenetic protocol when animals consumed a high sugar diet resulted in lower eating and a protection from diet-induced obesity.
source: However, applying the same optogenetic protocol when animals consumed a high sugar diet resulted in lower eating and a protection from diet-induced obesity.
evidence: Demonstrated through optoFLIC and TAG assay experiments (Figure 4A-D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)

claim: Variations in relative PAM DANs activity, rather than their absolute output, may modulate feeding behavior in flies exposed to high dietary sugar.
source: Since these neurons have lower activity in flies on a high sugar diet, we propose that the optogenetic stimulation in this context functions as a normalization of the activity, rather than activation in the absence of the stimulus. This suggests that variations in relative PAM DANs activity, rather than their absolute output, may modulate feeding behavior in flies exposed to high dietary sugar.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the differential effects of optogenetic stimulation on CD vs SD

claim: Sensory-enhanced satiation plays an early role in the satiety cascade before post-oral nutrient-derived signals consolidate satiety.
source: Studies in rodents and humans have delineated the importance of sensory signals to modulate satiation and terminate meals. This process, termed sensory-enhanced satiation (Chambers et al., 2015), plays an early role in the satiety cascade before post-oral nutrient-derived signals consolidate satiety (Bellisle and Blundell, 2013; Blundell et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chambers et al., 2015; Bellisle and Blundell, 2013; Blundell et al., 1987

claim: Higher sensory intensity and oral exposure promote stronger satiation.
source: Data show that higher sensory intensity and oral exposure promote stronger satiation (Bolhuis et al., 2011; Ramaekers et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bolhuis et al., 2011; Ramaekers et al., 2014

claim: High sensory characteristics, such as saltiness and sweetness, enhanced the satiating effect of both low and high energy test drinks.
source: For example, high sensory characteristics, such as saltiness and sweetness, enhanced the satiating effect of both low and high energy test drinks (Yeomans and Chambers, 2011; Yeomans et al., 2014), decreased consumption of pasta sauce (Yeomans, 1998; Yeomans, 1996), yoghurt (Vickers et al., 2001) and tea (Vickers and Holton, 1998).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior human studies

claim: Sensory-enhanced satiation involves the central dopaminergic processing of peripheral sweet taste stimuli by a dedicated group of PAM-β'2 neurons.
source: Here we characterized the circuit-based mechanisms of sensory-enhanced satiation by exploiting the simplicity of the fruit fly system. We show that sensory-enhanced satiation involves the central dopaminergic processing of peripheral sweet taste stimuli by a dedicated group of PAM-β'2 neurons.
evidence: Demonstrated through the combination of imaging and behavioral experiments in this study

claim: Satiation may involve a learning or rewarding component.
source: Given the role of PAM DANs transmission in reinforcing appetitive memories (Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012), this discovery is significant because it suggests that satiation may involve a learning or rewarding component and that diet composition may direct food intake by influencing this aspect.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on known roles of PAM DANs and current findings

claim: Diet composition may direct food intake by influencing the learning or rewarding component of satiation.
source: Given the role of PAM DANs transmission in reinforcing appetitive memories (Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012), this discovery is significant because it suggests that satiation may involve a learning or rewarding component and that diet composition may direct food intake by influencing this aspect.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on known roles of PAM DANs and current findings

claim: Sensory cues function as a predictor of nutrient density and set expectations for how filling different types of foods should be.
source: Indeed, sensory cues function as a predictor of nutrient density and set expectations for how filling different types of foods should be (Chambers et al., 2015; McCrickerd and Forde, 2016; Yeomans, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chambers et al., 2015; McCrickerd and Forde, 2016; Yeomans, 2017

claim: PAM DANs promote the formation of short-term associative memories based on taste by modulating plasticity of the postsynaptic Mushroom Body Output Neurons (MBONs).
source: In fruit flies, PAM DANs promote the formation of short-term associative memories based on taste and long-term associative memories based on nutrient density by modulating plasticity of the postsynaptic Mushroom Body Output Neurons (MBONs) (Cohn et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cohn et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015

claim: PAM DANs promote the formation of long-term associative memories based on nutrient density by modulating plasticity of the postsynaptic Mushroom Body Output Neurons (MBONs).
source: In fruit flies, PAM DANs promote the formation of short-term associative memories based on taste and long-term associative memories based on nutrient density by modulating plasticity of the postsynaptic Mushroom Body Output Neurons (MBONs) (Cohn et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cohn et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015

claim: MBONs are connected to pre-motor areas like the Central Complex.
source: MBONs are, in turn, connected to pre-motor areas like the Central Complex (Aso et al., 2014a) – the fly genetic and functional analog of the basal ganglia (Strausfeld and Hirth, 2013) – providing an anatomical route to modulate aspects of feeding such as proboscis extension (Chia and Scott, 2019), the analogue of licking or chewing rate.
evidence: Supported by citations to Aso et al., 2014a; Strausfeld and Hirth, 2013; Chia and Scott, 2019

claim: The Central Complex is the fly genetic and functional analog of the basal ganglia.
source: MBONs are, in turn, connected to pre-motor areas like the Central Complex (Aso et al., 2014a) – the fly genetic and functional analog of the basal ganglia (Strausfeld and Hirth, 2013) – providing an anatomical route to modulate aspects of feeding such as proboscis extension (Chia and Scott, 2019), the analogue of licking or chewing rate.
evidence: Supported by citation to Strausfeld and Hirth, 2013

claim: Some MBONs receive input from both the taste (β'2) and nutrient (γ5) compartments.
source: Interestingly, some MBONs receive input from both the taste (β'2) and nutrient (γ5) compartments, raising the possibility that sensory and nutrient memories may be integrated in the same cells to regulate different aspects of the satiety cascade (satiation vs. satiety).
evidence: Based on known anatomical connectivity

claim: The mode and timing of DA delivery onto the MBONs is critical to establish the strength and valence of the associations.
source: In flies, the mode and timing of DA delivery onto the MBONs is critical to establish the strength and valence of the associations (Handler et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Handler et al., 2019

claim: The delay and decrease measured in animals on a high sugar diet could impair MBON synaptic plasticity and the formation of new appetitive memories.
source: The delay and decrease we measured in animals on a high sugar diet could impair MBON synaptic plasticity and the formation of new appetitive memories (Cohn et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on known roles of DA timing and current findings

claim: By reducing peripheral taste sensation, a high sugar diet impairs the central DA processing of sensory signals and weakens satiation.
source: In conclusion, our experiments demonstrate that by reducing peripheral taste sensation, a high sugar diet impairs the central DA processing of sensory signals and weakens satiation.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of all experimental results in the study

claim: These studies forge a causal link between sugar, taste sensation, and weakened satiation.
source: These studies forge a causal link between sugar – a key component of processed foods – taste sensation, and weakened satiation, consistent with the fact that humans consume more calories when their diets consist of processed foods (Hall et al., 2019).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results and supported by citation to Hall et al., 2019

claim: Humans consume more calories when their diets consist of processed foods.
source: These studies forge a causal link between sugar – a key component of processed foods – taste sensation, and weakened satiation, consistent with the fact that humans consume more calories when their diets consist of processed foods (Hall et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hall et al., 2019
